questions.q: What does a tenant-wide governance status dashboard actually show?
options: Only the names of Power BI reports with no other detail
Domains, workspaces, and item counts, plus coverage signals like how much content has a description or was recently accessed
Only the tenant admin's personal activity
A list of every DAX formula used across the tenant
questions.explain: The governance status view summarizes the whole estate: domain/workspace/item counts alongside coverage measures like descriptions and last-access dates.

questions.q: According to this lesson, how does 'items by last access date' on the governance dashboard relate to earlier chapters?
options: It's unrelated to anything covered earlier in the course
It's the same idea as Lesson 14's usage metrics, applied across the whole tenant instead of one report
It replaces the need for an audit log entirely
It only applies to Power BI Desktop files
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly connects this estate-wide access metric to the usage-metrics concept from Lesson 14, just rolled up to tenant scale instead of one report.

questions.q: What do 'recommended actions' on the enterprise governance surface actually provide?
options: Vague, abstract advice with no specifics
Concrete, specific tasks like structuring data by domains or raising sensitivity label coverage
A list of users to fire for non-compliance
Automatic deletion of all uncertified content
questions.explain: Recommended actions are concrete and specific — things like 'Establish sources of truth with endorsements' or 'Increase sensitivity label coverage,' directly actionable rather than abstract.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say real enterprise scale (hundreds of workspaces, thousands of items) matters for how governance mechanisms are designed?
options: Because at that scale, governance becomes unnecessary
Because no single person could manually check every item by hand, so every mechanism this course covered has to scale down to one judgment call and roll up into one tenant-wide view
Because Power BI stops working above a certain number of items
Because enterprise scale means certification is automatically disabled
questions.explain: At real scale — over a hundred workspaces and thousands of items — manual, item-by-item review isn't feasible, which is exactly why mechanisms like endorsement, labeling, and lineage are designed to work at the individual level but aggregate into one dashboard.

questions.q: Which of these correctly matches an earlier chapter to its enterprise-scale counterpart described in this lesson?
options: Chapter 1 (workspaces) has no enterprise-scale equivalent
Workspaces (Chapter 1), sensitivity/trust (Chapters 2-3), and lifecycle/pipelines (Chapter 4) all roll up into the same tenant-wide governance surface
Only Chapter 4 content appears in enterprise governance; earlier chapters are unrelated
Enterprise governance is a completely separate topic unconnected to any previous chapter
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly maps workspaces, sensitivity and trust, and lifecycle/pipelines — spanning all four chapters — onto the same enterprise-wide governance dashboard.
